meta.blurb: For twenty years Charles Darwin quietly collected facts. Then a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace arrived with the same idea, and he rushed to write. Here is the book that argues nature, not a breeder, picks who survives.
meta.bible: Charles Darwin: English naturalist, born 1809, who sailed on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836 and later lived and worked at Down House in Kent. On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection: his book, published by John Murray in London on 24 November 1859; the full title adds 'or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life'. Alfred Russel Wallace: a naturalist working in Ternate who in 1858 wrote to Darwin about the same idea. Charles Lyell and Joseph Hooker: Darwin's friends, who arranged for both men's ideas to be read at the Linnean Society in July 1858. The book has an Introduction and fourteen chapters; Darwin called it 'one long argument'. Its only picture is one Diagram of a branching tree. Key terms: Species, Variation, Domestication, Breeders, Selection, Natural Selection, Struggle for Existence, Malthus (Thomas Malthus, a writer on populations), Divergence, Instinct, Hybrids, Sterile, Fossils, Geological, Extinction, Embryos, Rudimentary, Descent, Evolved, Fantail, Pouter, Tumbler, Pigeons, Rock Pigeon, Peacock, Cuckoo, Honeybee, Hexagonal, Wallace, Tangled Bank, Galapagos, Armadillos, Sloths, Vertebrates, Naturalists, Creation, Wolves, Lyell, Hooker, Linnean, Beagle, Kent, Ternate, Murray, Mammals, Pollinate, Clover, Humble-bees, Nectar, Hereditary, Mankind. Darwin is careful and modest in the text: he lists his own difficulties and says where he does not know. This book retells the argument faithfully, adds no invented numbers or quotes, and says plainly where Darwin or later science is uncertain. Voice: clear, patient and wondering, like a good teacher who respects both Darwin and the reader.

beats.scene: An open book on a table beside a quill and a magnifying glass
beats.summary: In the Introduction, Darwin says species have not been made separately but have changed over time.

beats.summary: Chapter III: more young are born than can possibly survive, an idea Darwin takes from Thomas Malthus.

beats.scene: Lines link a cat, a mouse, a bumblebee and a clover flower

beats.scene: Two similar finches fight over one seed on a branch
beats.summary: The struggle for life is fiercest between close relatives, who need the same food and places.

beats.scene: A mouse with slightly longer legs escapes a hawk while others are caught
beats.summary: Chapter IV: a small difference that helps an animal live and have young is more likely to be passed on.

beats.scene: A breeder's hand and a mountain landscape, with a tiny hawk circling

beats.scene: A blind white fish and a pale beetle in a dark cave
beats.summary: Chapter V: parts that are used grow stronger, and parts that go unused may shrink; animals in dark caves can be blind.

B1B2: As a young man, Charles Darwin spent nearly five years sailing around the world on a ship called the Beagle. Everywhere he went, he noticed how many different kinds of living things there are.
After the voyage, Darwin settled in a quiet house in Kent. For about twenty years he gathered facts and tested his ideas, because he wanted to be very sure.

In 1858 Darwin received a letter from a naturalist called Alfred Russel Wallace, who was working far away in Ternate. Wallace had reached almost the same idea, so Darwin's friends arranged for both men's work to be read together in London.

Darwin now wrote his book as fast as he could, although he called it only a short summary of his larger plan. It was published in London on 24 November 1859, with a long title that began On the Origin of Species.

In his Introduction, Darwin explains that he believes species were not each made separately. Instead, he thinks they have changed slowly, and that natural selection is the most important way this happens.
Darwin starts with animals and plants that people look after. Dogs, cattle, horses and wheat all come in many varieties, and no two animals are exactly the same.
Darwin kept pigeons himself and joined clubs of pigeon fanciers. Some breeds, such as the fantail, the pouter and the tumbler, look so different from each other that they seem to be separate species.

Yet Darwin argues that every fancy pigeon came from a single wild bird, the rock pigeon that lives on sea cliffs. Sometimes, when two very different breeds are crossed, the young look like that wild bird again.

The secret of the breeders is selection, which is the idea behind all their work. They choose the animals with the feature they like and breed from them, and after many generations the tiny differences grow big.
Selection does not always need a plan, and farmers often do it without knowing. For hundreds of years they have kept their best animals and sold the poorest, so the herds changed without any goal.
In his second chapter, Darwin turns to the wild. Here too, no two creatures are exactly alike, and the small differences between them may be passed on to their young.

Naturalists have never agreed on what exactly a species is, and this is a real problem. Experts often argue about whether two kinds are separate species or only varieties of one, because the line between them is blurred.
Darwin suggests that a well-marked variety is a young species still in the making. Common and widespread kinds, which have many members, seem to show the most variety.
In the third chapter, Darwin points out something simple. Every kind of living thing makes far more young than can possibly survive, an idea he took partly from the writer Thomas Malthus.

Even the slowest breeders would soon fill the world if all their young lived. Darwin chose the elephant, which has very few babies, and showed that in under a thousand years one pair could have millions of descendants.

Food, weather, enemies and disease all keep numbers down, and they are tangled together. Darwin's famous example is clover, which needs bumblebees; mice destroy bumblebee nests, and cats eat the mice.

Darwin uses the word struggle in a wide sense, and it does not always mean a fight. The hardest struggle of all is between creatures of the same kind, because they need exactly the same food and the same places.
Now Darwin joins his two ideas together to make a new one. If a small difference helps an animal live longer and have more young, and if its young inherit it, that feature will spread.

Darwin called this process natural selection, because it works like the breeder's choice but without any breeder. Nature has no plan, yet it is patient: it can work on every part of a creature, over countless years.
Darwin imagines a pack of wolves in a hard winter, when food is scarce. The swiftest and cleverest wolves would catch the most deer, so they would survive best and pass those gifts to their young.
Darwin adds a second kind of choosing, called sexual selection. Males may fight over females, or females may prefer the most colourful males, and this may explain the peacock's wonderful tail.
Darwin warns that natural selection works very slowly, over thousands of generations. We cannot watch the changes while they happen, and we only see the result after a very long time.
Darwin explains that descendants which differ from each other can live in more places and eat more kinds of food. So one kind of creature gradually splits into several, and then into many more.
The book contains just one picture, a diagram of lines that spread like the branches of a tree. It shows how a few kinds, over time, can give rise to many, while some branches die out.

In chapter five, Darwin looks at the laws of variation, which he says are little understood. He thinks that parts used a lot may grow stronger and parts never used may shrink, as in blind cave animals.

Darwin also notices that some features seem to change together, in ways that are hard to explain. For example, white cats with blue eyes are very often deaf, which shows that different parts of the body can be linked.
In chapter six, Darwin does something unusual: he lists the difficulties of his own theory. The first is why we do not see many forms in between one species and the next.
Next comes the eye, which has many parts that work together perfectly. Darwin admits that it seems absurd to think natural selection could make it, but he says a feeling is not a good argument.

Darwin points to living animals, which have eyes of every kind, from a simple spot that senses light to a sharp and complex eye. Each step is useful to the animal that has it, so a slow path to a perfect eye is quite possible.

Darwin gives other examples of gradual change, such as flying squirrels, which glide between trees on a fold of skin. Different squirrels have more or less of this fold, so a path of small improvements is easy to imagine.

Chapter seven is about instinct, which Darwin says can vary and be inherited, just like a body. His examples are the cuckoo, which lays eggs in other birds' nests, and ants that make other ants work for them.

Darwin was especially charmed by the honeybee, whose wax comb is made of perfect six-sided cells. He suggests that bees reach this clever shape through simple instincts that save wax, which was costly for the bees to make.
In chapter eight, Darwin discusses hybrids, the young of two different species, like a mule. Hybrids often cannot have young, but Darwin shows that this rule is not perfectly strict.
Darwin compares the record in the rocks to a book of the world's history in which most of the pages are lost. Only a few chapters survive, and in those chapters only a few lines can still be read.
Darwin explains why so few creatures became fossils, since a body must be buried quickly in mud or sand. Land animals seldom meet this fate, and the time involved is enormous, so much remains unseen.

In chapter ten, Darwin shows that fossils are found in order, with the oldest at the bottom and the newest at the top. He also notices that the fossils of a place often look like the living animals of that place.
Darwin also writes about extinction, the end of a kind of living thing. A species usually becomes rare first, he says, so we should not be surprised, just as sickness comes before death.

In chapters eleven and twelve, Darwin looks at where plants and animals live. Two lands may have the same weather but quite different living things, which fits the idea of descent from nearby ancestors.

To see how plants might reach distant islands, Darwin did experiments, and he soaked seeds in salt water for weeks. Many still sprouted, and he also showed that seeds can travel in mud on a bird's feet.

Darwin noticed that far-off islands have almost no frogs or land mammals, but they have many birds and insects. The living things on an island are usually like those of the nearest mainland, which supports his idea.
In chapter thirteen, Darwin looks at how we sort living things. They fall naturally into groups within groups, like boxes inside boxes, which is just what we expect if all are related.

Darwin asks us to think about a human hand, a bat's wing, a horse's leg and a porpoise's flipper. They do very different jobs, yet they are built from the same bones in the same order, which suggests a shared ancestor.

Darwin also notes that the very young embryos of different animals, such as a fish, a bird and a mammal, look alike. As they grow, they begin to differ, and he sees this as another sign that they share ancestors.
Many animals have small parts that they do not use, like the tiny wings of birds that cannot fly. Darwin compares them to letters we still write in a word, although we no longer say them.

In the last chapter, Darwin goes over the whole argument again. He reminds the reader that many different kinds of facts, from breeding, fossils, maps and bodies, all seem to point in the same direction.
Darwin knew that many experienced naturalists would not agree with him. He hoped that younger scientists, who were still open to new ideas, would weigh both sides of the question fairly.
Darwin said very little about human beings in this book. He wrote only that light would be thrown on the origin of man and his history, and he left a fuller discussion for later books.
Near the end, Darwin pictures a tangled bank covered with plants, with birds in the bushes and worms in the damp earth. All these different living things, he says, have been shaped by the same laws.

Darwin's last words are about grandeur, and he sees something grand in the idea that life began in a few simple forms. From so simple a start, he says, endless beautiful forms have been, and still are being, evolved.
The book sold very quickly, and booksellers bought the whole first printing of about 1,250 copies almost at once. Darwin kept improving the text, and it was printed in six editions in his lifetime.
C1C2: In the early years of his manhood, Charles Darwin sailed around the world aboard the Beagle and studied every creature, plant and rock he could lay his hands on. What he saw on that long journey planted a question in his mind that would not go away. It was a question about where the countless kinds of living things on Earth had come from.

Once the voyage was over, Darwin settled in a quiet country house in Kent, where his study slowly filled with notebooks, specimens and letters. For about twenty years he gathered evidence and tested his ideas against it, for he knew that his theory would meet fierce opposition. He was a cautious man, and he preferred to be certain before he said anything in public.

In the summer of 1858, a letter reached Darwin from a naturalist named Alfred Russel Wallace, who was working in the distant island town of Ternate. To Darwin's alarm, it described very nearly the same theory that he had been nursing in secret for two decades. His friends Charles Lyell and Joseph Hooker settled the matter generously by having both men's ideas read together to a scientific society in London.

Spurred on by Wallace's letter, Darwin set about writing his book at last, and he called the result a mere summary of a much larger work he had in mind. It was published by John Murray in London on 24 November 1859, under the title On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection. Darwin himself described the whole thing as one long argument, and that is the best way to read it.

In his Introduction, Darwin declares that he has come to believe that species are not unchanging, nor was each one made separately and set down on Earth fully formed. They have descended, with modification, from earlier kinds, and he proposes natural selection as the chief, though not the only, means of that change. The rest of the book, he promises, will set out the facts and let the reader judge.

Darwin begins not in the wild but at home, with the animals and plants that people have kept for ages. Dogs, cattle, horses and garden flowers appear in an astonishing range of forms, and even within a single litter no two puppies are exactly alike. This, he argues, is the raw material from which every change in nature is ultimately built.

To study variation closely, Darwin kept pigeons in his own garden and made friends among the fanciers who bred them for show. The fantail spreads its tail like a peacock, the pouter swells its chest into a great round balloon, and the tumbler throws itself into somersaults in the air. Their shapes differ so strongly that a naturalist, finding them in the wild, would surely call them separate species.

Yet all these breeds, Darwin concludes, descend from one wild ancestor, the grey rock pigeon that nests on cliffs and in caves. His evidence is persuasive: when two very different breeds are crossed, their young sometimes revert to the colours and markings of the wild bird. It is a strong clue that quite different forms can spring from one origin, given enough time.

The breeders' secret, Darwin explains, is selection, and it is simpler than it sounds. A fancier picks the birds that show a little more of the feature he admires, allows only those to raise young, and repeats this through many generations until tiny differences have grown into striking ones. Man does not make the variation, but he decides which of it will be kept.

Darwin adds that selection is often unconscious, practised by people who have no thought of altering their stock at all. Century after century, farmers have kept their finest animals and parted with their weakest, and in doing so they have gradually reshaped whole breeds. Nobody set out to build the modern sheep, yet the sheep were built all the same.

Having shown how much living things vary at home, Darwin turns in his second chapter to the wild, where he finds the same restless variety. No two beetles, birds or flowers are quite identical, and many of their small differences are handed down from parent to young. Variation, in other words, is not a quirk of tame creatures but a feature of life itself.

Darwin observes that naturalists have never agreed on a definition of the word species, and he shows how often experts quarrel over whether two forms are distinct species or merely varieties. If the dividing line were truly sharp, he reasons, such quarrels could not arise. The line is blurred, and that blurring is exactly what we should expect if varieties are species in the making.

From this he draws a bold conclusion: a well-marked variety is a species that has not yet finished forming. He notes that the larger, more widespread and more successful groups tend to produce the most varieties, as though they were the busiest workshops of change. What we call a species, then, is only a stage along a road, and not a fixed and final thing.

The third chapter turns on a plain but sobering fact: every living thing produces more offspring than the world has room to feed. Darwin borrowed the heart of this idea from the writer Thomas Malthus, who had studied how human populations press against their supplies of food. In nature, Darwin says, the same pressure is at work everywhere and all the time, though we seldom notice it.

Even the slowest breeder on Earth, Darwin shows, would soon overrun it if every offspring lived to have young of its own. He chose the elephant, which bears very few calves in a long life, and calculated that a single pair could leave millions of descendants within about seven hundred years. Since the world is plainly not packed with elephants, most of those that are born must die before they can breed.

What keeps numbers in check, Darwin explains, is a web of causes, from hunger and frost to enemies and disease, all tied together in surprising ways. His best-known illustration runs from cats to mice, from mice to the nests of humble-bees, and from those bees to the clover that depends on them for pollination. Near a village with many cats, he suggests, there may therefore be more clover.

Darwin takes care to use the word struggle in a broad and metaphorical sense, which includes depending on another being and succeeding in leaving young, not only fighting. The fiercest competition, he adds, is between close relatives, since creatures of the same kind want the same food, the same shelter and the same mates. A slight advantage over a neighbour can therefore matter enormously, even when it looks like nothing at all.

At the heart of the book stands the fourth chapter, where Darwin joins his earlier ideas into one. If a slight variation helps an animal to survive and to leave offspring, and if that feature is inherited, then it will tend to spread through the population generation by generation. Harmful variations, on the other hand, will tend to vanish, since their owners seldom live to breed.

Darwin named this process natural selection, in deliberate echo of the breeder's art, though in nature there is no breeder and no plan. The choosing is done by life itself, by hunger, weather and enemies, and it never rests, which gives it the advantage of unlimited time. Where a fancier looks only at outward show, nature, he says, works on every part of the inner and outer body, and on every shade of difference.

To make his idea vivid, Darwin pictures wolves living on the edge of hunger, in a season when their prey is hard to find. The swiftest and most cunning wolves would surely catch the most deer, and so they would be the ones to survive and rear young that shared their speed. After many such winters, he reasons, the whole pack might become faster, without any wolf having tried to change.

Darwin also describes a second and related process, which he calls sexual selection, and which depends not on survival but on success in finding a mate. When males battle one another for females, or when females prefer the brightest and boldest of them, the winning traits are inherited by the young. The peacock's glittering tail, a burden in many ways, may well have grown by such a contest.

Natural selection, Darwin cautions, works with infinite slowness, so slowly that we cannot watch it in progress and can only judge the results. We see nothing of these gradual alterations, he says, until the hand of time has marked the long lapse of ages. The difficulty lies in imagining the span of time, not in the idea itself.

Why do living things branch into so many different forms rather than change in a single direction? Darwin answers that descendants which differ from one another can occupy more different places in nature, find more kinds of food and compete less with their own relatives. In this way, one kind slowly divides into several, and each of those divides again, as the branches of a tree do.

The entire book contains only one illustration, a diagram in which lines fan out and divide across the page like the limbs of a tree. It shows how a few ancient kinds could give rise to a great many descendants over long ages, while many lines stop short and are lost for good. Darwin later compared the whole of life to a great tree whose green twigs bud and grow while the dead branches fall away.

The fifth chapter looks into the laws of variation, and here Darwin is frankly modest about how little is understood. He suggests that a part which is much used may grow stronger and one that is neglected may dwindle, and he points to the many blind animals of dark caves as a possible case. Darwin admits, however, that the real causes of variation are mostly hidden from us, and he does not pretend otherwise.

He also observes that the body behaves as a whole, so that a change in one part is often accompanied by a change in another, for reasons nobody then understood. His favourite oddity was the white cat with blue eyes, which is very frequently deaf as well. Such links show that variation is not a matter of single features altering in isolation.

The sixth chapter is remarkable because Darwin sets out the objections to his own theory with unusual honesty. The first is obvious: if species have changed by small steps, why are we not surrounded by countless in-between forms? He replies that the improved forms tend to replace the older ones they came from, so the links are usually lost.

Next he confronts the eye, an organ of such delicate perfection that it seems impossible for it to have arisen by gradual steps. Darwin freely admits that the very idea seems, at first sight, absurd in the highest possible degree, yet he insists that a feeling is not a proof. If the steps can be shown to exist, and each one is useful to its owner, the difficulty begins to disappear.

Darwin points out that the animal kingdom today offers a whole ladder of eyes, from a mere spot of light-sensitive nerve to the keen lens of a hawk or a human. Every rung of that ladder is useful to the creature that owns it, and each might be improved a little by selection over an immense period. He does not claim to know exactly how any particular eye arose, but he shows that the road is not closed.

To show that striking abilities may begin modestly, Darwin turns to the flying squirrels, whose loose folds of skin allow them to glide from tree to tree. Among the squirrels living today there is a graded series, from kinds with a slight fold to kinds with a wide gliding membrane, and each is well suited to its way of life. It is therefore easy to picture a long chain of small improvements, each one a little better than the last.

In the seventh chapter Darwin argues that instincts, like bodily features, vary from one individual to another and are passed down, so that selection may shape them too. He examines the cuckoo, which lays its eggs in the nests of other birds and whose chick pushes the rightful young out, and an ant that raids its neighbours to carry off workers. These behaviours, he says, could have grown by small steps, each of some advantage.

Darwin was captivated by the honeybee, whose comb is a marvel of six-sided cells fitted together without wasted space. He argues that the bees do not need to be mathematicians, since a few simple habits, refined by selection over many generations, are enough to produce the pattern. Those that used the least wax would have stored the most honey, so even this instinct bears the stamp of gradual improvement.

The eighth chapter deals with hybrids, the offspring of two different species, such as the mule, whose parents are a horse and a donkey. It had long been argued that such young are always sterile, proving that species were made separate, but Darwin shows that the rule is far from strict and varies widely from case to case. A barrier that comes in degrees, he says, is just what slow change would produce.

Chapter nine takes up the fossil record, which Darwin likens to a history of the world, imperfectly kept and written in a changing dialect. Of that history we possess only the last volume, he says, and of this volume only a few short chapters have survived, with a line or two from each page. It is no wonder, then, that the story shows so many gaps in its telling.

To become a fossil, Darwin explains, a creature must be buried quickly in mud or sand, and left undisturbed for ages, which happens only rarely and mostly under water. Land animals, which seldom meet such a fate, are far less often preserved, so the record leans heavily towards sea creatures. We should therefore expect large gaps, and not take them as proof against his idea.

Chapter ten shows that fossils lie in a definite order through the layers of rock, the oldest forms below and the more recent above, with species coming and going one by one. Darwin also notes that the extinct animals of a region usually resemble the living animals there, as the bones of giant armadillo-like creatures in South America recall the armadillos that still live on that continent. He had seen such bones himself on his voyage, and the memory clearly stayed with him for the rest of his life.

Extinction, Darwin writes, is the natural companion of selection, for as new forms are favoured the older and less fit forms give way. A species commonly becomes rare before it disappears, and he sees nothing mysterious in that, any more than we marvel when a sick person grows weaker before dying. The truly surprising thing, he suggests, is that we ever expected species to last forever.

In the eleventh and twelfth chapters, Darwin examines how living things are scattered across the globe, and he notices that similar climates in different continents do not carry similar creatures. Barriers such as seas, deserts and mountain ranges seem to matter more than the weather, and each region is populated mainly by the descendants of its own earlier inhabitants. That pattern, he says, is exactly what descent from nearby ancestors would lead us to expect.

How could plants have crossed wide stretches of ocean to reach remote islands, far from any other land? Darwin tested the question himself, soaking seeds in salt water for weeks and finding that a surprising number still sprouted when he planted them. He also showed that a little mud on a bird's foot can carry seeds across great distances, so that the sea is no absolute barrier.

Darwin noticed that remote oceanic islands rarely have native frogs or land mammals, yet they are often rich in birds, insects and plants that could cross the water. The creatures found there are generally related to those of the nearest mainland, as the animals of the Galapagos Islands resemble those of South America. The simplest explanation, he says, is that they are descendants of a few arrivals that changed in their new home.

The thirteenth chapter considers classification, the habit of sorting living things into groups nested inside larger groups, as boxes are packed inside boxes. Naturalists had long used this pattern without explaining it, but Darwin argues that its cause is simple: the groups reflect real family relationships. Species that share more recent ancestors are placed closer together on the branching tree.

Consider, Darwin says, the hand of a man, the wing of a bat, the leg of a horse and the flipper of a porpoise, which serve such different purposes. Nonetheless they are built on the same pattern of bones arranged in the same order, a similarity that is hard to explain by the needs of each animal. It makes perfect sense, however, if all were adapted from the limbs of a common ancestor.

Darwin turns next to the embryos of different animals, which, in their earliest stages, are strikingly similar, whether they will become fish, birds, reptiles or mammals. Only later in their growth do they diverge into the forms of their kind, as though each carried a faint memory of a shared beginning. He takes this as yet another sign that these animals are descended from a common stock.

Many creatures carry rudimentary organs, small and useless parts such as the tiny wings of birds that cannot fly. Darwin compares them to the silent letters still written in a word, which are kept because they show where the word has come from. Such leftovers are puzzling if every creature was made separately and perfectly, but they are easy to understand as the faded remains of what ancestors once used.

In the final chapter, Darwin gathers the threads of his argument and goes over them once more. Breeding, geography, fossils, anatomy and the growth of embryos, he points out, are very different fields of knowledge, yet they all lead to the same conclusion. It is the fact that so many separate lines of evidence converge that gives the theory its strength.

Darwin did not pretend that his case was complete, and he expected that many experienced naturalists, long used to another view, would reject it. His hope lay with the younger generation, who would be able to look at both sides of the question without prejudice. He asked only for a fair hearing, and he promised nothing more than honest argument.

Darwin was careful to say very little about our own species in this book, for he knew how deeply the subject would disturb his readers. A single short remark promises that light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history, and nothing more. He took up the matter at length in a later work, The Descent of Man, published in 1871.

In his closing paragraph Darwin invites us to look at a tangled bank, thickly covered with many kinds of plants, with birds singing in the bushes, insects flitting about and worms crawling through the damp earth. These elaborate forms, so different from one another and yet so dependent on each other, have all been produced by laws acting around us. It is a picture that is at once ordinary and astonishing, and he leaves it for the reader to ponder.

The book closes on a note of wonder, for Darwin finds grandeur in the view that life, with all its powers, began in a few forms or perhaps only one. While the planet has gone on turning according to the fixed law of gravity, he writes, endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have grown from so simple a beginning. The very last word of the book, remarkably, is evolved, a word he used hardly anywhere else in it.

The first printing of about 1,250 copies was bought up by booksellers almost at once, and the book soon became the subject of passionate argument in newspapers, lecture halls and drawing rooms. Darwin never stopped revising it in response to his critics, and it went through six editions in his lifetime. Later discoveries, above all in the science of genes, which he knew nothing about, have corrected and enriched his ideas, yet the core of his argument remains the foundation of modern biology.
